tier_reason: README Benchmarks section gives first-party hyperfine and strace -c tables against GNU ls 9.7, busybox 1.36.1, eza, lsd and uutils with versions, but no benchmark script, CPU model, kernel or build flags; first-party with partial methodology is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: hyperfine, directory of n plain files, '-al': n=10,000 lsr 22.1 ms vs GNU ls 38.0 ms (1.72x, derived from page data), busybox 32.5 ms, eza 40.2 ms, uutils 89.6 ms, lsd 153.4 ms; n=10 lsr 372.6 us vs ls 1.4 ms (3.8x, derived from page data). strace -c at n=10,000: 848 syscalls vs 30,396 for GNU ls.
corrections.caveats: First-party; CPU, kernel, filesystem and cache state not stated; no benchmark script in the README; a tool comparison (io_uring-batched statx) rather than a library. The relative gap versus GNU ls is largest at small n (3.8x at n=10) and narrows to 1.72x at n=10,000; busybox is close at every size. io_uring batching only on Linux; macOS/BSD builds get no syscall benefit.

notes: All numbers match the README tables exactly. The record's caveat that smaller directories narrow the gap was backwards and is corrected. Metadata (MIT, 52 stars, last commit 2026-09-19) checked on github.com.

tier_reason: The README states qualitatively that NOVA outperforms other DAX file systems in almost all cases (sub-page updates excepted) and defers numbers to the FAST'16 paper; the paper PDF (usenix.org) was egress-blocked, so the peer-reviewed numbers were seen only in search snippets and B cannot be confirmed here.

corrections.claimed_speedup: FAST'16 paper abstract (search snippet only): in write-intensive workloads 22% to 216x throughput improvement over state-of-the-art file systems and 3.1x to 13.5x over file systems with equally strong consistency guarantees. README: outperforms other DAX-enabled file systems in almost all cases; sub-page updates are an exception (whole-page COW).
corrections.caveats: Paper (Xu and Swanson, FAST'16, https://www.usenix.org/conference/fast16/technical-sessions/presentation/xu) blocked in this environment; numbers from search-result snippets of the abstract. Out-of-tree Linux 5.1 kernel tree, GPL-2.0 WITH Linux-syscall-note; self-described as not production ready (no mkfs/fsck, no xattrs, x86-64 only). Needs NVMM/DAX hardware or emulation. Last commit 2022-02-21.

notes: Candidate for a paper-access retier to B: the FAST'16 abstract's 22%-216x and 3.1x-13.5x figures were confirmed by two independent search snippets but the USENIX PDF returned a proxy 403. Last commit 2022-02-21 is over 3 years old, so abandoned.

tier_reason: README 'Sample Performance' tables give first-party wall times versus GNU tar on GPFS with no benchmark script, CPU, versions or flags; C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Linux kernel source (1.5 GB, 47K files, GPFS hot page pool, no compression): gnutar 6m4s vs 64 workers 9.4 s (about 38.7x, derived from page data), 128 workers 9.9 s, 1 worker 6m33s; 10 TB 500K-file dataset: gnutar 10hr20m vs 32 workers 44m39s (about 13.9x, derived from page data), 32 workers with gzip 8hr22m.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers on a parallel file system with a hot page pool; 1 worker is slower than GNU tar (6m33s vs 6m4s); no flags, versions or CPU given. Output is many separate valid tar files, not one archive, so it is not a drop-in replacement; parallel decompression not done. Last commit 2019-10-31.

notes: Numbers match the README. Metadata checked: MIT/Expat stated in the README (no LICENSE file at root), 15 stars, last commit 2019-10-31 (abandoned).
